subjects.question: Who made a prosperous capital—and whose movement was coerced?
subjects.summary: Isfahan’s squares, workshops and markets connected court authority with craft and long-distance trade. Silk involved growers, dyers, weavers, merchants and consumers. New Julfa’s Armenian community became important to this economy after forced deportation from the old town. Keeping that coercion visible changes the meaning of a beautiful carpet: wealth and artistic skill did not arise outside politics or unequal power.

sections.title: A capital grows within an older city
sections.text: The conventional transfer of the Safavid capital falls in 1597–98. Haneda and Matthee distinguish a gradual transformation from a single instant of creation, and a mobile royal household from a modern permanently resident government. The new square, shops, caravansaries and covered bazaar formed a commercial and governmental center alongside older urban life. The city did not begin when the shah selected it.

citations.locator: Isfahan as the Safavid Capital: proclamation, mobile household, new square and commercial center

sections.title: Silk has a chain of work
sections.text: Raw silk from northern provinces passed through several kinds of labor before becoming luxurious cloth. Munroe distinguishes rural producers, court workshops and private urban workshops, including dyers, weavers and embroiderers. Designers planned repeated patterns, while weaving transformed threads into a surface. The Doria carpet shows costly material and repeated design; its museum record names several cities for the type rather than proving where this individual carpet was woven.

citations.locator: Workshop organization, Caspian raw silk and weaving processes

sections.title: Trade cannot erase deportation
sections.text: Ghougassian describes the destruction of Old Julfa and forced Armenian movement during the Ottoman–Safavid war in 1604. New Julfa took shape at Isfahan in 1605. Some merchants later gained privileges and built institutions, but later commercial achievement does not make the initial movement voluntary. The record also distinguishes wealthier merchants from other deportees and describes changing restrictions. No single experience stands for everyone moved by the state.

sections.title: Check the collecting name
sections.text: The carpet type was once attributed to Poland and called Polonaise. The Met now identifies Iranian production in workshops including Isfahan, Yazd and Kashan. A later label can preserve collecting history while misleading us about manufacture. We can inspect the silk and metallic brocading without inventing a named weaver, an exact export itinerary, or a specific workshop that the catalogue does not establish.

subjects.question: What changes when a book, a market and a reservoir are read together?
subjects.summary: Bukhara was a place of government, learning and trade long before 1500. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century building added madrasas, commercial spaces and water infrastructure to that older city. A manuscript probably painted there lets us look at a different kind of skilled work. Its copied text, later painting and much older poem remind us that a book does not have only one date or one place.

sections.title: An older city, active new building
sections.text: UNESCO identifies much of Bukhara’s surviving urban fabric with Uzbek rule from the sixteenth century onward, alongside earlier monuments. Pugachenkova and Rtveladze describe active building under the Shaibanids and Janids: bazaars, caravansaries and reservoirs as well as religious institutions. Trade with Russia expanded during these periods. This evidence does not support treating Central Asia as a static space between other empires.

citations.locator: Shaibanid 1500–98 and Janid 1599–1785 periods; trade and urban construction

sections.title: Learning and exchange used built spaces
sections.text: The Mir-i Arab madrasa dates to 1535–36 in the archaeological account. Other foundations and covered commercial structures followed. Rooms for students, markets for merchants and reservoirs for water served different activities within the same city. Their presence helps us ask about daily work and infrastructure, but does not give us the biography or experiences of every student, seller or water carrier.

citations.locator: Mir-i Arab; Qush Madrasa; domed commercial structures and reservoirs

sections.title: Several makers and several moments
sections.text: The illustrated Bustan folio is attributed to Shaikh Zada. The catalogue says the manuscript was likely copied in Herat, then illustrated for an Uzbek patron, probably in Bukhara in the 1530s. Sa‘di’s poem is older still, completed in 1257. Text composition, copying and painting are separate acts. The qualified terms likely and probably are part of the evidence, not inconveniences to be removed for a tidier map.

sections.title: A reception is a literary image
sections.text: Patterned textiles, architecture and expensive objects help create the depicted scene. They are evidence of choices made by the artist and patron, not a photograph of every Bukharan household. Comparing this book with Iznik ceramics or Isfahan textiles can expose shared questions about skill, patronage and use. Similarity alone does not prove a direct transfer between two particular workshops.

interval.note: Dynastic convention follows Perry. Karim Khan’s residence in Shiraz from 1765–1779 is narrower; the 1789 case belongs after his death and is not assigned to his personal use.

subjects.question: Can a small case reveal work and taste without becoming a portrait of an entire reign?
subjects.summary: After the disruptions of the earlier eighteenth century, Karim Khan made Shiraz a center of rule and building. Merchants and artisans contributed to urban life, while campaigns and political limits remained part of that history. A lacquer case dated 1789 carries the investigation beyond Karim Khan’s lifetime. Its practical compartments and painted courtly scene offer different kinds of evidence.

sections.title: A title and its limits
sections.text: Perry describes Karim Khan’s rule from 1751 to 1779 and his residence at Shiraz from 1765. He used the title wakil, or deputy, rather than shah. This language matters for political representation, but it does not make his government a modern elected system. His authority did not include all territories associated with earlier Iranian rulers, and military campaigns remained a means of enforcing power.

citations.locator: Karim Khan, the Wakil: dates, title, territory and campaigns

sections.title: Building and buying in Shiraz
sections.text: The scholarly account describes merchants from Europe and India, rebuilding, gardens, a covered bazaar and artisans drawn to Shiraz. Such work helps explain a capital beyond its ruling household. At the same time, a court observer’s pleasant reminiscence cannot establish that every resident prospered. Buildings, commercial agreements and personal narratives must each be read for the question they can actually answer.

citations.locator: The Wakil at Shiraz, 1765–79: commerce, rebuilding, artisans and Donboli’s recollection

sections.title: The case is dated after the ruler’s death
sections.text: The Met attributes the lacquer case to Muhammad Baqir and dates it 1204 AH/1789 CE. It therefore cannot be labeled a possession made for Karim Khan, who died in 1779, without separate provenance. Its drawer was arranged for a dressing set, while the painted lid includes a courtly gathering. A function, an artistic subject and a named maker are three different claims.

sections.title: Observe closely without inventing a story
sections.text: The outside’s birds and flowers differ from the gathering inside. Both involve skilled surface-making as well as the work of constructing a useful container. The museum identifies Iran but not a secure city of manufacture. We can compare this late-eighteenth-century object with the earlier carpet and manuscript without inventing an unbroken workshop lineage, a particular party, or a known purchaser.
